t: You're listening to Ah Beng Podcast. I'm Maya.
And I'm Guy. Today, a geopolitics special: the machines that print every advanced chip on Earth, and the case for cutting China off from them.

This one's from ChinaTalk, Jordan Schneider's newsletter, published October twentieth. The piece is called The Lithography Lever — the case for cutting China off from deep ultraviolet lithography, or D-U-V.

Jordan co-hosts with Ah-keeb Zakaria, and their guest is Nick Brown, co-founder of the Center for Technology and Statecraft, a new think tank spun out of I-F-P. He wrote a monster report called D-U-V Immersion Lithography: The Foundation of U-S A-I Compute Advantage — and Jordan calls it his paper of the year.
Big claim. So let's set the table. Why should we care how much compute China has?

Because compute is one of the three drivers of A-I capability — compute, algorithms, and data — and Nick's point is that it's the most governable of the three. It's the lever you can actually pull. The number of chips, their quality, the total stock — that shapes who can exercise A-I power, economically, militarily, across the board.
Alright, tale of the tape, October twenty twenty-six. Where do the two sides stand?
Everyone's numbers are hazy, but at the median estimate the U-S lead is commanding. In H-one-hundred equivalents, China has maybe a million chips. The U-S has upwards of thirty million.
Ten to one. And that's before the asterisks.
Right — there's almost another million in remote-access compute China can reach in data centers in Thailand, Malaysia, and elsewhere in Southeast Asia. Which shows you how hard this is to measure.
Okay, but here's the part of the conversation that really landed for me: leverage. Not all chips are equal.

This is Nick's key frame. Three segments. Chips China accesses remotely — high leverage, the U-S could cut that off any morning. Chips that were exported — some leverage, but once it's shipped, it's gone. And chips China manufactures itself — almost zero leverage.
And that third category is the whole ballgame. If China can print its own A-I chips, the chokepoint stops being a chokepoint.
Exactly. So while everyone argues about how many Nvidia chips to sell, the real question is what China can build at home.
Which brings us to lithography. We already banned the extreme ultraviolet machines, E-U-V, right? Isn't this a solved problem?

That's what they call the cannonball-sized hole in export controls. E-U-V gets all the press — those machines cost hundreds of millions each, and by many measures they're the most advanced technology on the planet. But D-U-V, deep ultraviolet — sixty to eighty million dollars a machine — is still extraordinarily powerful.
How powerful?
The most advanced D-U-V system, the A-S-M-L N-X-T nineteen-eighty-i, is good enough for seven-nanometer logic and H-B-M memory — which is exactly what Huawei's Ascend A-I chips use.
So China doesn't need E-U-V to build A-I chips.

No. And they've exploited the gap. Nick's team estimated China imported about ninety immersion systems a year in twenty twenty-four and twenty-five — worth over ten billion dollars, nearly two-thirds of A-S-M-L's entire immersion exports.
Ninety a year. And the total installed base?
About three hundred and forty A-S-M-L lithography systems inside China today. In hindsight, Nick calls letting that many flow in a strategic loss.
Alright, so play the movie forward. Exports keep flowing, the machines install, and there's no leverage once they're in. Where does China land in five or ten years?

Two findings from the report. First: the current stockpile — huge as it is — is physically incapable of matching U-S A-I chip production through twenty thirty-five. Even if China diverted every machine to its best fabs and spent one hundred percent of capacity on A-I, not a single smartphone, they'd get something like a tenth of U-S output.
Because lithography throughput is just physics — a fixed number of wafers per machine per year.

Right. But finding two: if imports continue at the twenty twenty-four rate, the curve bends. There are scenarios — U-S production tapers, China accelerates and goes all-in on A-I — where you're looking at near parity, maybe parity, within a decade.
From a guaranteed ten-to-one advantage to a coin flip.
At minimum, a much smaller advantage with real uncertainty about the whole computational balance of power. That's the stakes.
Now the obvious counter: can't China just build their own lithography machines? They're indigenizing everything else.

That's the thing — lithography is the one segment where China has zero percent market share, and it's almost certainly the hardest and the last tool they'll crack. Etch, deposition, metrology — those are coming; C-S-E-T reports show real progress. But Nick's team is confident China won't make D-U-V good enough for A-I chips at scale until into the twenty thirties.
And they stress-tested that. What if China pulls off a miracle?

He ran a hyper-aggressive scenario — a seven-nanometer-capable prototype next year, faster than A-S-M-L ever managed, commercial production the year after, one hundred percent growth every single year. Even then, the stockpile plus indigenous production never gets close to U-S-allied output.
So the door stays shut even in the fantasy case. Okay — enter Congress. What is the M-A-T-C-H Act?

Bipartisan, both chambers, and it's sitting in the Senate version of the N-D-A-A right now, so it gets fought over in conference over the next couple of months. Two buckets. Bucket one: countrywide controls on the really big semiconductor equipment — including D-U-V immersion lithography — upgrading them from entity restrictions to blanket bans. No more of it enters China at all.
And bucket two?

Alignment. The U-S already blocks all of its own equipment from China's most advanced fabs — SMIC and C-X-M-T. Japan and the Netherlands block only a small set. M-A-T-C-H tells the allies to match U-S controls. That's literally the name.
And the mechanics?

The Commerce Department gets about a hundred and fifty days to negotiate with the allies, because controlling Dutch and Japanese tools through their own governments is the cleaner solution. But if talks fail, B-I-S imposes the controls unilaterally. They've done it before.
What about servicing? A-S-M-L and Tokyo Electron engineers are all over Chinese fabs keeping the machines alive.

Nick treats exports and servicing as separate dials. The item ban is the big, decade-scale move. Servicing restrictions bite faster and messier — expect degradation in yield and throughput maybe six to twelve months out, starting with the light sources, the stages, and the sensors. Though he'd bet against production actually stopping — a lot of that work would just shift to Chinese contractors.
His nuance there was interesting: go after the advanced fabs, leave the legacy ones alone.

Right — advanced nodes are sixteen or fourteen nanometers and below, where A-I chips get made. Legacy fabs don't make A-I chips, and servicing them is where the toolmakers earn most of their maintenance revenue. Spare the legacy fabs and the political blowback shrinks.
Now, the stockpiling question. A hundred and fifty days of warning sounds like a hundred and fifty days to go shopping.

They will. Remember, a single N-X-T nineteen-eighty-i can produce over a hundred thousand Ascend chips a year, even with China's lousy yields. Nick expects tens of systems — maybe over a hundred — to land before the act takes effect.
Doesn't that kill the whole thing?

No, and this is the key mental shift. The chip-export fights are month-to-month — how many H-ones did Huawei get this quarter. M-A-T-C-H hits the fundamental chokepoint for a decade. Even if a hundred machines slip through first, cutting off the flow after that caps China's ceiling for ten years or more.
And the smartphone worry? People everywhere use Huawei phones.

Nick's answer: with three hundred forty machines already in country, China has enough lithography for all its smartphone demand for the next decade. The only thing big enough to saturate that capacity is enormous A-I chipmaking. So the collateral damage story mostly doesn't apply.
Okay, the big geopolitical question. Does Beijing torch the relationship over this? Rare earths summer, part two?

Jordan called that the strongest argument against the act, and Nick's answer is about the form of the law. Executive export controls can be done and undone when some appointee sends an email. An act of Congress is still law — even a hostile administration can't be sure the next one won't enforce it. That changes the game theory.
And the timeline matters too.

Right — the pain is slow. China won't feel the import ban next week, next month, or even next year. There's nothing instantaneous to retaliate against. Jordan's image: this is a mute on the violin, not smashing it. It passes right as Xi and Trump meet, and by the time it bites it's a fifteen-year drip, not a tariff shock.
Plus there's a fun hidden lever in the report — the light sources.

Every immersion machine on Earth uses a light source from one of two companies: Cymer, which is American — A-S-M-L owns it, but it's based in the U-S, and, quote, we had it first — or Gigaphoton in Japan. Which means the U-S and Japan alone, no extraterritorial magic needed, can control every D-U-V immersion tool headed to China.
The whole semiconductor century runs through two lightbulb factories.

Ha — two very, very fancy lightbulbs. One more political-economy point: M-A-T-C-H is great news for chipmakers across the allied world. If Huawei and C-X-M-T output floods out of China, it eats the margins of Samsung, S-K Hynix, Nvidia, A-M-D, Intel. Controlling it protects them.
So where does this rank for people who think compute policy is really about remote access and distillation?

Nick's verdict: on anything five or ten years out, lithography is his golden baby — number one. Because the foundation of strategic advantage is indigenous chipmaking, and the foundation of that is litho.
And his bottom line?

Cut the imports and you close the door on anything approaching U-S-China parity. His words: it's a button that lets you win the A-I competition, at least as measured by chipmaking. Keep them flowing and that guarantee just isn't there.
The episode ends with Ah-keeb — who'd been wavering the whole interview — finally put on the spot. Gun to your head?
His answer: let's rock and roll, baby. Let's pass the M-A-T-C-H Act. And Jordan's reply — the clock's ticking, it's October, and this Congress is ending.
That's the episode. The full piece is The Lithography Lever, on ChinaTalk — show notes have the link. Thanks for listening to Ah Beng Podcast.
See you next time.
